prompt:
Carbon forms two different oxides. In oxide A, 1.000 g of carbon is combined with 1.332 g of oxygen. In oxide B, 1.000 g of carbon is combined with 2.664 g of oxygen.

For a fixed mass of carbon, what is the ratio of oxygen masses, B : A? Enter it as a decimal.
hints: Two different compounds made of the same two elements: that is the setting of the Law of Multiple Proportions (Day 1 p.13).
The law compares the mass of one element that combines with a fixed mass of the other.
Carbon is already fixed at 1.000 g in both oxides, so you can compare the two oxygen masses directly.
Ratio = (2.664 g O) ÷ (1.332 g O). The grams cancel, leaving a pure number.
solution:
Ratio (B : A) = 2.664 g ÷ 1.332 g = 2.000. That is a 2 : 1 ratio of small whole numbers, exactly what the Law of Multiple Proportions predicts (Day 1 p.13).

At the particle level, oxide B carries two oxygen atoms for every one that oxide A carries, per carbon atom. Atoms combine only in whole numbers (Dalton, Day 1 p.14), so the oxygen mass can only change in whole-number steps.

The simplest formulas that fit are CO and CO2. Choosing actual formulas needs more information than this ratio gives.

compare.wrong: “Oxide A is 1.332 ÷ 2.332 = 57.1% O and oxide B is 2.664 ÷ 3.664 = 72.7% O. Then 72.7 ÷ 57.1 = 1.27, which isn’t a whole number, so the law fails.”
compare.tempting: Percent composition is the method from Day 1 p.11, so reaching for it feels natural.
compare.fails: Percentages change the basis: each percentage is out of a different total mass. The law compares one element's mass per fixed mass of the other element. Fix carbon at 1.000 g and the ratio is exactly 2 : 1.

label: lecture

prompt: Pure water is always 11.2% hydrogen by mass (Day 1 p.11). A sample of pure water contains 3.00 g of hydrogen. What is the mass of the water sample?
hints: Same compound means same composition: this is the Law of Constant Composition.
Mass fraction of H = (mass of H) ÷ (mass of water) = 0.112.
Rearrange: mass of water = (mass of H) ÷ 0.112.
Mass of water = 3.00 g ÷ 0.112.
solution: Mass of water = 3.00 g ÷ 0.112 = 26.8 g (3 significant figures, matching 3.00 g and 11.2%). Check: 26.8 g × 0.112 = 3.00 g of H, so the rest, 23.8 g, is oxygen.
label: lecture

prompt:
Sulfur forms two oxides. In sample X, 1.00 g of sulfur is combined with 1.00 g of oxygen. In sample Y, 1.00 g of sulfur is combined with 1.50 g of oxygen.

For a fixed mass of sulfur, what is the ratio of oxygen masses, Y : X?
hints: Two compounds of the same two elements, so think multiple proportions.
Is the mass of one element already held fixed in both samples?
Yes: sulfur is 1.00 g in both, so compare the oxygen masses.
solution:
Ratio = 1.50 g ÷ 1.00 g = 1.50, a 3 : 2 ratio of small whole numbers.

This is the textbook's sulfur–oxygen example, SO3 vs. SO2 (textbook §1.1, PDF p.41, printed 7).
label: lecture

prompt: A 10.0 g sample of a white solid is heated in an open dish. A gas escapes, and 5.60 g of solid remains. Nothing else enters or leaves. What mass of gas escaped?
hints: Which law governs where the “missing” mass went?
Conservation of mass: matter is neither created nor destroyed (Day 1 p.10).
Total mass before = mass of the solid left + mass of the gas that escaped.
Mass of gas = 10.0 g − 5.60 g.
solution: Mass of gas = 10.0 g − 5.60 g = 4.4 g. For subtraction, the answer keeps the fewest decimal places: 10.0 has one, so report 4.4 g. The mass didn't disappear; it left as a gas. That is exactly why the law was hard to see for centuries: gas masses are hard to track (Day 1 p.10).
label: lecture

prompt: Which postulate of Dalton's atomic theory directly explains the Law of Multiple Proportions?

options.html: Matter consists of atoms, which cannot be destroyed.
options.feedback: That postulate explains conservation of mass: atoms are rearranged, not destroyed.

options.html: All atoms of the same element are identical to each other.
options.feedback: Identical atoms help explain why one compound has a fixed composition, but they don't by themselves produce whole-number ratios between two compounds.

options.html: Atoms combine in small whole-number ratios when forming compounds.
options.feedback: Right. If compound B has two O atoms for every one in compound A (per C atom), the oxygen mass must double: a small whole-number ratio.

options.html: Atoms of different elements have different masses.
options.feedback: True for Dalton (the second postulate says atoms of different elements differ), but different masses alone don't force whole-number ratios.

hints: Match each of Dalton's three postulates (Day 1 p.14) to the law it explains.
Multiple proportions is about whole-number ratios. Which postulate mentions whole numbers?
solution: Atoms combine in small whole-number ratios. That postulate makes the oxygen mass per fixed mass of carbon change in whole-number steps. The “cannot be destroyed” postulate explains conservation of mass, and “identical atoms” supports constant composition.
label: lecture

prompt:
Nitrogen forms several oxides. Per 1.00 g of nitrogen, compound I contains 0.571 g O, compound II contains 1.14 g O, and compound III contains 2.28 g O.

What is the ratio of oxygen masses, III : I? Then decide whether all three compounds obey the same law.
hints: The mass of one element (nitrogen) is fixed, so multiple proportions applies.
Divide each oxygen mass by the smallest one.
Round each result to the nearest small whole number and check that it's close.
solution:
III : I = 2.28 ÷ 0.571 = 3.99 ≈ 4, and II : I = 1.14 ÷ 0.571 = 2.00 ≈ 2. The oxygen masses are in the ratio 1 : 2 : 4, all small whole numbers, so all three compounds obey the Law of Multiple Proportions.

Formulas consistent with 1 : 2 : 4 are N2O, NO, and NO2 (O per g N: 16.00/28.01 = 0.571; 16.00/14.01 = 1.14; 32.00/14.01 = 2.28).
label: lecture

prompt: In two or three sentences: why does the Law of Constant Composition make sense if matter is made of atoms?

answer.model: Every unit of a pure compound contains the same number of each kind of atom, and all atoms of one element have the same mass (Dalton, Day 1 p.14). So every sample, of any size, has the same mass ratio of its elements. Water is always 11.2% H because every water unit has the same H and O atoms (Day 1 p.11).

label: lecture

prompt: “Every sample of table salt, from any source, is 39.3% sodium by mass.” Which law does this illustrate?

options.feedback: Right: one compound, always the same composition by mass.
That law needs two different compounds of the same two elements.
That law is about total mass before and after a change.
Energy isn't mentioned; this is about composition.

hints: One compound or two? Composition or a before/after comparison?
solution: Constant Composition. One compound always has the same proportion of its elements by mass (Day 1 p.11).

prompt: A student reports that a sample of pure water is 20% hydrogen by mass. What is the best conclusion?

options.html: Water's composition depends on where it came from.
options.feedback: That would violate constant composition, which holds for every pure compound.

options.html: The sample isn't pure water, or the measurement is wrong.
options.feedback: Right: pure water is always 11.2% H by mass (Day 1 p.11).

options.html: The hydrogen atoms in this sample are heavier.
options.feedback: Dalton: all atoms of one element are identical (Day 1 p.14). Isotopes change masses only slightly and don't explain 20% (RAMP UP, Day 2 p.23).

options.html: Some mass was destroyed during the measurement.
options.feedback: Mass is conserved (Day 1 p.10).

hints: What does the Law of Constant Composition promise about every pure sample?
solution: Pure water is always 11.2% hydrogen by mass. A 20% result means the sample isn't pure water, or the measurement went wrong.

prompt: Using the particle table from Day 2 p.22 (proton 1.00728 amu; electron 5.48580 × 10−4 amu), how many electrons would it take to equal the mass of one proton?
hints: Compare masses, not charges.
Number of electrons = (mass of a proton) ÷ (mass of an electron).
Both masses are in amu, so the units cancel.
solution: 1.00728 ÷ (5.48580 × 10−4) = 1,836, so about 1836 electrons weigh as much as one proton. That's why Thomson concluded the cathode-ray particles were “TINY” (Day 2 p.10), and why Day 2 p.12 says a hydrogen atom is about 2000 times heavier than an electron (the exact figure is about 1837).

compare.wrong: “The table lists charges of +1.60218 × 10−19 C and −1.60218 × 10−19 C. Their sizes are equal, so it takes 1 electron.”
compare.tempting: Charge and mass sit side by side in the table, and the charges really are equal in size.
compare.fails: Charge and mass are different properties. Equal-and-opposite charges are why a hydrogen atom is neutral; the masses differ by a factor of about 1836.

label: lecture

prompt: In a cathode-ray tube, the beam bends toward the positively charged plate. What does that tell you about the particles in the beam?

options.feedback: Like charges repel, so a positive beam would bend away from the + plate.
Right: opposite charges attract (Day 2 p.10).
A neutral beam wouldn't bend in an electric field at all.
Light isn't bent by charged plates; this beam is (Day 2 p.7).

hints: Which way do opposite charges move toward each other?
solution: Negatively charged. The beam is attracted to the + plate (Day 2 p.7, p.10).

prompt: Which gold-foil observation could the plum-pudding model NOT explain?

options.html: Most α particles passed straight through the foil.
options.feedback: Both models predict that: the atom is mostly open to a fast α particle (Day 2 p.16–17).

options.html: A few α particles bounced back at large angles.
options.feedback: Right: spread-out positive charge can't turn a heavy α particle around. A tiny, concentrated nucleus can (Day 2 p.15–17).
That's a property of the α particle, not something the foil experiment revealed.

options.html: The gold foil was very thin.
options.feedback: That's part of the setup, not an observation that tests a model.

hints: Compare the predicted paths in the plum-pudding picture (Day 2 p.16) with the nuclear picture (Day 2 p.17).
Which result is the “15-inch shell … came back and hit you” surprise (Day 2 p.15)?
solution: The few large-angle bounce-backs. In the plum-pudding atom every α path goes nearly straight through (Day 2 p.16). A bounce-back requires a tiny, dense, positive nucleus (Day 2 p.17–19).
label: lecture

prompt: In the Day 2 p.20 figure, a gold atom is about 288 pm across and its nucleus about 0.01 pm. If the nucleus were enlarged to the size of a 1.0 cm marble, about how wide would the atom be, in meters?
hints: This is a scale (ratio) problem, so keep the ratio of the two sizes the same.
Atom ÷ nucleus = 288 pm ÷ 0.01 pm.
Multiply that ratio by the new nucleus size, 1.0 cm.
288 ÷ 0.01 = 28,800, so the atom would be 28,800 cm. Now convert to meters.
solution:
288 pm ÷ 0.01 pm ≈ 2.9 × 104, so the atom is about 28,800 cm ≈ 288 m across. That's roughly three football fields around a marble. With 0.01 pm known to only one significant figure, “about 3 × 102 m” is the honest answer.

The sources disagree slightly: Day 2 p.19 says the nucleus is “about 1/10,000” the size of the atom, while the figure's numbers give about 1/29,000. Both are order-of-magnitude statements (~10−4).
label: lecture

prompt: RAMP UP (self-study) A neutral carbon-13 atom (13C) has how many protons, neutrons, and electrons?
hints: An element's identity is set by its number of protons (Day 2 p.24). Carbon is element 6.
The mass number, 13, counts protons + neutrons.
Neutrons = 13 − 6.
A neutral atom has as many electrons as protons.
solution: 6 protons, 7 neutrons, 6 electrons. 13C is an isotope of carbon with one “extra” neutron compared with 12C (Day 2 p.23).
label: lecture

prompt: In a modified Thomson-style tube, a beam bends toward the negative plate. At the same speed, it takes a much stronger magnet to bend this beam than to bend cathode rays. What can you conclude about the particles?

options.feedback: A negative beam would bend toward the + plate.

options.html: Positive and much more massive per unit charge than electrons
options.feedback: Right: attraction to the − plate means positive charge, and resisting the magnet means more mass per unit of charge.
Neutral particles wouldn't bend toward either plate.
Lighter particles would be easier to bend, not harder.

hints: First use the direction of the bend to find the sign of the charge.
Then think about what makes a moving particle harder to deflect.
solution:
They're positively charged (attracted to the − plate) and much heavier per unit charge than electrons (harder to bend). This reverses Thomson's reasoning on Day 2 p.10.

Beams like this are positive ions, historically called “canal rays.”
label: lecture

prompt: Explain why most α particles went straight through the gold foil but a few bounced back.

answer.model: The atom is mostly empty space: a diffuse cloud of very light electrons that can't deflect a heavy α particle. Nearly all the mass and all the positive charge sit in a tiny nucleus, roughly 10−4 of the atom's width (Day 2 p.19–20). Most α particles never pass near a nucleus. The rare one headed almost straight at a nucleus feels an enormous repulsion and is thrown back (Day 2 p.15–18).

label: lecture

prompt: Match each experiment to what it revealed.
hints: Day 2 p.12 and p.14 list the three experiments in order.
solution:
Thomson → tiny negative particles in all atoms (Day 2 p.10). Millikan → the electron's charge and mass, qe = −1.602 × 10−19 C (Day 2 p.12). Rutherford → the nucleus (Day 2 p.14).

Strictly, the oil drops measured the charge; combining it with Thomson's charge-to-mass ratio gave the mass.
label: lecture

prompt: A classmate says the α particles that bounced back must have hit electrons. What's wrong with that?

options.html: Nothing; electrons are what the α particles hit most.
options.feedback: Electrons are far too light to reverse a heavy α particle.

options.html: Electrons are about 1/1836 of a proton's mass, far too light to turn a heavy α particle around.
options.feedback: Right: only the massive, positive nucleus can do that (Day 2 p.12, p.22).

options.html: Electrons are positively charged, so they'd attract α particles.
options.feedback: Electrons are negative (Day 2 p.10).
Electrons are inside the atom, in a diffuse cloud (Day 2 p.17).

hints: Compare the electron's mass with the proton's (Day 2 p.22).
solution: An electron has about 1/1836 of a proton's mass (Day 2 p.22). It can't reverse a heavy α particle; only the massive nucleus can.
label: lecture

prompt: Green light has a wavelength λ = 5.30 × 102 nm. Find (a) its frequency and (b) the energy of one photon.
hints: Light: wavelength ↔ frequency through c; photon energy through h (Day 2 p.30; Day 3 p.17).
λν = c, so ν = c/λ. Then E = hν.
Convert λ to meters first: 5.30 × 10<sup>2</sup> nm × (10<sup>−9</sup> m / 1 nm) = 5.30 × 10<sup>−7</sup> m.
solution:
ν = c/λ = (2.998 × 108 m/s) ÷ (5.30 × 10−7 m) = 5.66 × 1014 s−1.

E = hν = (6.626 × 10−34 J·s)(5.66 × 1014 s−1) = 3.75 × 10−19 J per photon.

Units: m/s ÷ m = s−1; J·s × s−1 = J. Three significant figures, set by 5.30 × 102 nm. Sanity check: visible light sits near 1014–1015 Hz on the spectrum (Day 2 p.29), and this value does.

compare.tempting: The wavelength is given in nm, and it's easy to plug the number straight in.
compare.fails: c is in m/s, so λ must be in meters. 5.66 × 10<sup>5</sup> Hz is a radio frequency on the Day 2 p.29 spectrum, not green light. A unit mismatch shows up as an impossible region.

label: lecture

prompt: Rank these from highest photon energy (1) to lowest (5).
hints: Energy per photon rises with frequency and falls with wavelength: E = hν = hc/λ.
The spectrum on Day 2 p.29 runs from “Shortest wavelength (Highest energy)” (γ rays) to “Longest wavelength (Lowest energy)” (radio).
solution: γ rays > ultraviolet > red light > infrared > microwaves. Shorter wavelength means higher frequency, which means more energy per photon (Day 2 p.29).
label: lecture

prompt: An FM radio station broadcasts at 98.5 MHz (1 MHz = 106 s−1). What is the wavelength?
hints: Frequency to wavelength for light (any EM radiation): λν = c.
λ = c/ν.
solution: λ = c/ν = (2.998 × 108 m/s) ÷ (9.85 × 107 s−1) = 3.04 m, radio waves a few meters long, consistent with the “Radio” band on Day 2 p.29.
label: lecture

prompt: A photon carries 4.41 × 10−19 J. What is its wavelength in nanometers, and what color is it?
hints: Energy of one photon ↔ wavelength.
E = hc/λ, so λ = hc/E.
Convert meters to nm by dividing by 10<sup>−9</sup> m/nm.
solution: λ = hc/E = (1.986 × 10−25 J·m) ÷ (4.41 × 10−19 J) = 4.50 × 10−7 m = 450 nm. That's blue on the visible scale (Day 2 p.29 shows 450 nm as blue).
label: lecture

prompt: If you double the wavelength of light, what happens to its frequency and to the energy of each photon?

options.feedback: λν = c is fixed, so if λ goes up, ν must go down.
Right: ν = c/λ halves, and E = hν halves with it.
E = hν, so energy follows frequency, not wavelength.

options.html: Nothing changes, because light always travels at c.
options.feedback: The speed stays c. That's exactly why ν must change when λ does.

hints: Hold c fixed in λν = c.
Energy follows frequency: E = hν.
solution: Both halve. c is constant, so ν = c/λ drops by half, and E = hν drops by half too.
label: lecture

prompt: A microwave oven uses 2.45 GHz radiation (2.45 × 109 s−1). How many microwave photons carry the same total energy as one ultraviolet photon of wavelength 2.50 × 102 nm?
hints: You need the energy of one photon of each kind.
Microwave: E = hν. UV: E = hc/λ.
Number of microwave photons = E<sub>UV</sub> ÷ E<sub>microwave</sub>.
solution:
Emicrowave = 1.62 × 10−24 J; EUV = 7.95 × 10−19 J. Ratio = 4.89 × 105: nearly half a million microwave photons to match one UV photon.

That's why microwaves warm food by sheer number of photons, while a single UV photon carries enough energy to do chemistry, even to damage molecules.
label: lecture

prompt: Explain why wavelength and frequency are inversely related for light.

answer.model: Every electromagnetic wave travels at the same speed, c. Frequency counts how many crests pass a point each second, and wavelength is the distance between crests. So crests per second × meters per crest = meters per second: λν = c (Day 2 p.30). With c fixed, a longer wavelength must mean fewer crests per second.

label: lecture

prompt: “A laser emits photons that each carry 3.00 × 10−19 J. What color is the laser?” Which relationship do you need first?

options.html: E = hc/λ, to get λ, then read the color off the spectrum
options.feedback: Right: λ = hc/E = 662 nm, which is red.
That's the de Broglie wavelength of a moving mass. A photon's energy uses E = hc/λ.
No metal or ejected electron is involved.
No hydrogen energy levels are involved.

hints: What object carries the energy: a photon, an electron in a metal, a hydrogen atom, or a moving mass?
solution: A photon's energy ↔ wavelength: E = hc/λ gives λ = 662 nm, which is red light (Day 2 p.29).
label: lecture

prompt: A student calculates that green light (530 nm) has a frequency of 5.66 × 105 Hz. What is the most likely error?

options.feedback: Even a slightly different c wouldn't cause a 10<sup>9</sup> error.

options.html: Wavelength left in nm instead of converted to m
options.feedback: Right: that's off by exactly 10<sup>9</sup>. Visible light is about 10<sup>14</sup>–10<sup>15</sup> Hz.

options.html: Used E = hν instead of λν = c
options.feedback: The result is a frequency, so the student did use λν = c, just with the wrong units.

options.html: Nothing; that's a reasonable visible frequency
options.feedback: Day 2 p.29 puts visible light near 10<sup>14</sup>–10<sup>15</sup> Hz.

hints: Compare the answer with the frequency scale on the Day 2 p.29 spectrum.
solution: The wavelength was left in nm. 5.66 × 105 × 109 = 5.66 × 1014 Hz is the right value.
label: lecture

prompt: A star's spectrum is a continuous rainbow crossed by dark lines at 656, 486, 434, and 410 nm. What can you conclude?

options.html: The star emits light only at those four wavelengths.
options.feedback: That describes an emission spectrum: bright lines on black. Here the lines are dark.

options.html: Hydrogen atoms in the star's outer layers absorb those wavelengths.
options.feedback: Right: dark lines on a continuous background mean absorption, and 656/486/434/410 nm are hydrogen's lines (Day 3 p.9–10).
Those are exactly hydrogen's wavelengths; the dark lines are hydrogen absorbing.

options.html: The dark lines are an artifact of the prism.
options.feedback: Wollaston and Fraunhofer saw the same lines with different instruments (Day 2 p.31).

hints: Start with the kind of spectrum: an unbroken rainbow, bright lines on black, or a rainbow crossed by dark lines?
Dark lines on a continuous background mean light is missing at specific wavelengths: the absence of light (Day 2 p.31). Something between the source and you absorbed it.
Which element has lines at 656, 486, 434, and 410 nm? Compare with the emission spectra on Day 3 p.9.
Those are hydrogen's four visible lines, and an element absorbs at the same wavelengths it emits (Day 3 p.10). So what is doing the absorbing, and where?
solution: The sun-like star emits a continuous spectrum, and hydrogen atoms in its atmosphere absorb specific wavelengths. That's the Kirchhoff explanation of Wollaston's dark lines (Day 3 p.10). The four wavelengths match hydrogen's four visible emission lines (Day 3 p.9).

compare.wrong: “Those four numbers are hydrogen's emission lines, so this is hydrogen's emission spectrum.”
compare.tempting: The wavelengths match hydrogen's emission lines exactly.
compare.fails: Emission appears as bright lines on a dark background. A continuous rainbow with dark gaps is an absorption spectrum. Same element, same wavelengths, opposite appearance (Day 3 p.8–10).

label: lecture

prompt: Match each description to the type of spectrum.

rows.html: A few bright colored lines on a black background
A complete rainbow with narrow black gaps
A complete rainbow with no gaps (a glowing hot solid)

hints: Bunsen and Kirchhoff's flames gave “very incomplete spectra with a few lines” (Day 3 p.8); white light through a sample gave rainbows “with characteristic gaps” (Day 3 p.10).
solution: Bright lines = emission; rainbow with gaps = absorption; unbroken rainbow = continuous (a hot solid, like the heated metal on Day 3 p.12).
label: lecture

prompt: Why were line spectra a problem for the physics of the early 1800s?

options.html: The lines were too faint to measure.
options.feedback: Fraunhofer measured them precisely (Day 3 p.7).

options.html: Existing theories couldn't explain WHY each element emits and absorbs only specific wavelengths.
options.feedback: Right: that's “The Limits of Classical Physics” (Day 3 p.11).
Prisms separated them fine; that's how the lines were found.

options.html: Every element had the same lines.
options.feedback: The opposite: each element has its own set (Day 3 p.9).

hints: See the “Limits of Classical Physics” slide (Day 3 p.11).
solution: Classical physics could describe the lines but not explain why an element emits and absorbs only certain wavelengths (Day 3 p.11). Quantization, starting with Planck, was the way out.
label: lecture

prompt: Hot hydrogen gas emits bright lines at 656, 486, 434, and 410 nm. White light is now passed through cold hydrogen gas and into a prism. Where do dark lines appear?

options.feedback: Right: the absorption and emission lines of an element coincide (Day 3 p.10 overlays them).

options.html: At four different wavelengths, shifted toward the red
options.feedback: Day 3 p.10 draws hydrogen's emission lines exactly on top of its dark absorption lines.

options.html: Nowhere; cold gas doesn't absorb light
options.feedback: Absorption is how Kirchhoff explained the dark lines in sunlight (Day 3 p.10).
That would be an emission spectrum seen in reverse; absorption removes only specific wavelengths.

hints: Look at the Day 3 p.10 figure, where hydrogen's emission lines are drawn over its absorption spectrum.
What does the atom need in order to absorb a photon, and is that any different from what it gives off when it emits?
solution: At the same four wavelengths. An element absorbs exactly the wavelengths it can emit, so its dark absorption lines sit where its bright emission lines would be (Day 3 p.10).
label: lecture

prompt: Connects to Module 3 One of hydrogen's visible lines is at 486 nm. What is the energy of one photon of that light?
hints: Each line is light of one wavelength, so each line is photons of one energy.
E = hc/λ (Day 2 p.30; Day 4 p.10).
Convert first: 486 nm = 4.86 × 10<sup>−7</sup> m.
solution:
E = hc/λ = (1.986 × 10−25 J·m) ÷ (4.86 × 10−7 m) = 4.09 × 10−19 J.

A line spectrum means hydrogen can only emit or absorb a few specific photon energies. Explaining why is exactly what the Bohr model does (Module 6, Day 4 p.10).
label: lecture

prompt: A glowing gas in a discharge tube shows bright lines at exactly the wavelengths where cold neon gas absorbs light. What's the best conclusion?

options.feedback: Right: an element emits and absorbs at the same wavelengths, so matching lines identify it.

options.html: The glowing gas is hydrogen, because all glowing gases emit hydrogen lines.
options.feedback: Each element has its own line pattern (Day 3 p.9).

options.html: Nothing; emission and absorption lines of one element never match.
options.feedback: They do match. Day 3 p.10 overlays hydrogen's emission and absorption lines.

options.html: The gas must be a mixture of every element.
options.feedback: One element's pattern accounts for the lines.

hints: What does Day 3 p.10 show about the positions of emission vs. absorption lines of the same element?
solution:
Line positions are an element's fingerprint, and emission and absorption lines coincide (Day 3 p.10). So the glowing gas is neon.

A cold gas absorbs mainly from its lowest energy level, so it shows fewer lines than the glowing gas emits, but every absorption line sits at one of the element's emission wavelengths.
label: lecture

prompt: Why do an element's absorption lines appear at the same wavelengths as its emission lines?

answer.model: Both involve the same allowed energy changes of the atom's electrons. Absorbing a photon lifts an electron up by one allowed gap; emitting a photon drops it down by the same gap. The photon's energy, and therefore its wavelength, equals that gap either way. (Bohr's model makes this explicit on Day 4 p.10; on Day 3 it was an unexplained observation, p.11.)

label: lecture

prompt: A student says the dark Fraunhofer lines prove the sun doesn't produce those wavelengths at all. What's the better explanation?

options.html: The sun produces a continuous spectrum, and elements in its atmosphere absorb those wavelengths.
options.feedback: Right: that's the partial explanation on Day 3 p.10.

options.html: The lines come from Earth's clouds.
options.feedback: The lecture attributes them to absorption by elements in the solar atmosphere.
Kirchhoff's absorption experiments showed the gaps come from absorption (Day 3 p.10).

options.html: The lines are wavelengths the prism can't bend.
options.feedback: Prisms bend all visible wavelengths.

hints: Day 3 p.10: “light is emitted continuously by the sun, but …”
solution: “Light is emitted continuously by the sun, but is absorbed by elements in the solar atmosphere” (Day 3 p.10).
label: lecture

prompt: Ultraviolet light with λ = 2.20 × 102 nm shines on a metal whose threshold energy (work function) is φ = 7.18 × 10−19 J. Is an electron ejected? If so, what is its kinetic energy?
hints: Light ejecting electrons from a metal is the photoelectric effect: KE = hν − φ (Day 3 p.19).
Find the photon's energy, E = hc/λ, and compare it with φ.
If E > φ, then KE = E − 7.18 × 10<sup>−19</sup> J.
solution:
E = hc/λ = (1.986 × 10−25 J·m) ÷ (2.20 × 10−7 m) = 9.03 × 10−19 J. That's larger than φ, so yes, an electron is ejected.

KE = hν − φ = 9.03 × 10−19 J − 7.18 × 10−19 J = 1.85 × 10−19 J.

Sig figs: in units of 10−19 J this is 9.03 − 7.18 = 1.85, and subtraction keeps two decimal places, so 3 significant figures here.

compare.wrong: “KE = hν + φ = 1.62 × 10−18 J. Also, a brighter lamp would make the electrons faster.”
compare.tempting: Adding feels natural (“the metal contributes energy”), and brighter light feels more energetic.
compare.fails: φ is the energy spent to free the electron; only the excess becomes kinetic energy (Day 3 p.19). Brightness means more photons, not more energy per photon, so it changes how many electrons are ejected, not how fast they move (Day 3 p.18).

label: lecture
